key_insight: Simulation-based reinforcement learning improved a language model’s psychiatric intake performance, outperforming its identically prompted base model in 76.7% of matched role-played scenarios.
clinical_relevance: The findings suggest potential for better history-taking, diagnostic reasoning, and patient-centered communication, but do not establish effectiveness in real-world patient care.
method: Trained a language model using multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulated psychiatric intake encounters.
Compared trained and base models in a randomized, double-blind crossover study with psychiatrist-enacted patients and independent psychiatrist scoring.
Stress-tested conversational safety using 256 adversarial presentations derived from Delphi-consensus taxonomies.
evidence_signal: In 60 matched scenario pairs (120 encounters), independent psychiatrists rated the trained model higher overall; adversarial testing also showed lower acute-risk under-triage (12.9% vs. 30.5%).
watch_item: Evaluation relied on simulated and psychiatrist-enacted encounters; residual safety failures require safeguards, clinician oversight, and real-world validation.
paper_title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
